Six Circles Theorem (Elkies)

GeometryCirclesTriangles
What it shows: A triangle with circles tucked inside it, one after another, and the seventh circle lands back on the first.
How to play: Drag a corner or the dot on the side, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Pick a pair of circles to colour, or show them all.
Colour which pair?
Look for the math

Drag the triangle about and the circles change size, but the chain never grows past six. That is the Six Circles Theorem, posed by Noam Elkies and proved by Jiro Fukuta.

Companion incircles

Cut a triangle from a corner to a point on the opposite side. You get two smaller triangles, each with its own incircle: these two are companions. Now cut again from the next corner along a tangent to the circle you just drew, and take the new incircle. The applet draws the first circle and then six more.

A rule every two circles obey

Let r be the big triangle's inradius, rn the radius of circle n, and hn the altitude from corner An. Demir's relation says

1/rn + 1/rn+1 − r/(rnrn+1) = 2/hn+2.

Write s for the semiperimeter. Since the triangle's area is both rs and anhn/2, the right side can be rewritten with the sides. Combining three such equations gives

(r/rn − 1)(r/rn+3 − 1) = tan²(an/2).

The logic test checks both equations at all six steps of hundreds of triangles; they hold.

Why six is the end

Replace n by n+3 in that last equation. The angle repeats every three corners, so the right side does not change:

(r/rn − 1)(r/rn+3 − 1) = (r/rn+3 − 1)(r/rn+6 − 1).

Because rn+3 < r, the common factor is not zero and can be cancelled: rn = rn+6. The chain of radii repeats after six. Our test also checks the stronger drawing fact: the seventh circle returns to the first one's centre and radius, so at most six distinct circles appear. A symmetric triangle can repeat earlier radii, but never more than six circles.

This page, and one small change

The applet has six "Show pair #" choices and "Show all circles"; we use one radio group so choosing a pair takes effect straight away. Its unused GetNextCircle and GetTouchingCircle routines are not copied, as nothing calls them. The applet lets point P reach a corner, where one incircle shrinks to nothing; here P stops a hair inside the side so the picture is always defined. Both changes are to the controls, not to the theorem. There is no win or loss: exploring the picture finishes a play.

Try Pair 3, then drag P close to A1: one circle in the pair becomes tiny while its companion stays large, yet the seventh circle still lands on the first.
